answer: BM25 scores a document for a query by summing, over the query terms, an idf weight times a saturating function of term frequency that is normalized by document length. Its two tuning parameters are k1 (about 1.2-2.0), which controls term-frequency saturation so the 10th occurrence of a word adds far less than the 2nd, and b (about 0.75), which controls length normalization. The idf factor is a smoothed inverse document frequency, so rare terms weigh more.

Reciprocal rank fusion runs lexical BM25 and dense retrieval in parallel and merges their result lists using only ranks, ignoring scores entirely. Each document's fused score is the sum over systems of 1/(k + rank), with k = 60 by convention. Because unbounded BM25 scores and cosine similarities are not comparable, RRF's rank-only combination needs no score normalization.

Nash proved in 1950 that every finite game has at least one equilibrium, possibly in mixed strategies, so an equilibrium always exists. But computing one is PPAD-complete (Daskalakis et al. 2009), which is believed intractable in the worst case. Existence therefore does not mean computability: an equilibrium can exist yet be unreachable by any efficient algorithm.

Forward mode carries a derivative alongside each value as a dual number, so one pass gives the derivative with respect to a single input and its cost scales with the number of inputs. Reverse mode (backpropagation) records the computation graph on a forward pass, then one backward pass propagates the output's derivatives back to every input at once via the chain rule. Its cost scales with the number of outputs, so for a scalar loss over millions of parameters it yields the entire gradient in a single backward pass, which is why deep learning uses reverse mode.

The Nyquist-Shannon theorem guarantees that a band-limited signal can be perfectly recovered if it is sampled at more than twice its highest frequency, the Nyquist rate. If you sample more slowly, aliasing occurs: frequencies above half the sample rate fold back and masquerade as lower frequencies that were never in the signal, as when a 20 kHz tone sampled at 30 kHz is heard as a 10 kHz tone. An anti-aliasing low-pass filter applied before sampling prevents this.

Assembly breaks every short read into overlapping k-mers and builds a de Bruijn graph whose nodes are (k-1)-mers and whose edges are the k-mers, each connecting its prefix to its suffix. The genome then corresponds to an Eulerian path that uses every edge exactly once, which is efficiently findable, unlike the NP-hard Hamiltonian-path formulation of older overlap-layout-consensus methods. The fundamental limit is repeats: repeat regions longer than k create tangles the graph cannot resolve, fragmenting the assembly.

In a second-price (Vickrey) auction the highest bidder wins but pays the second-highest bid, not his own. Since your bid only decides whether you win and never what you pay, bidding above your value risks paying more than the item is worth, while bidding below it risks losing a win that would have been profitable. Bidding your true value is therefore a dominant strategy.

BM25 is blind to the vocabulary mismatch problem: a query like 'heart attack' shares no terms with a document saying 'myocardial infarction'. Dense retrieval encodes queries and documents with a bi-encoder into a shared embedding space, so semantically similar text lands nearby and nearest-neighbor search matches meaning rather than exact keywords. Its weakness is that it can smear or miss exact and rare-term matches, which is why hybrid systems combine the two.

In 'No Silver Bullet' Brooks (1986) splits software difficulty into accidental complexity, which comes from our tools and can be removed, and essential complexity, which is inherent to the problem and irreducible. The order-of-magnitude gains of the past (high-level languages, time-sharing) worked by eliminating accidental difficulty. He argues no single advance will produce another order-of-magnitude gain because what remains is essential: the conceptual design of complex, changeable, invisible software entities.

PageRank imagines a random surfer who follows outlinks with damping factor d of about 0.85 and teleports to a random page with probability 1 - d, and it scores each page by its share of the surfer's stationary distribution. The scores are computed by power iteration, which costs O(edges) per step and converges in a few tens of iterations. Teleportation makes the Markov chain ergodic, which guarantees the stationary distribution exists and is unique.

Description logics reason under the open-world assumption: a fact that is not stated is unknown, not false, so the reasoner will not conclude that Alice has no other children merely because none are listed. This is the opposite of a database's closed-world assumption, where negation-as-failure treats anything not found as false. Description logics also make no unique-name assumption.

Columnar formats store each column's values contiguously, so a query that touches a few columns reads only those columns and can skip 10-100x of the data a row store would scan. Because values within a column are homogeneous, they compress far better with run-length encoding, dictionaries, and bit-packing, and min/max zone maps let whole blocks be skipped. The contiguous layout also lets vectorized (SIMD) execution process values in tight loops.
